1. Med Phys. 1998 Oct;25(10):2046-53. doi: 10.1118/1.598392.

Attenuation correction for a combined 3D PET/CT scanner.

Kinahan PE(1), Townsend DW, Beyer T, Sashin D.

Author information:
(1)Department of Radiology, University of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15213, USA. 
paul@pet.upmc.edu

In this work we demonstrate the proof of principle of CT-based attenuation 
correction of 3D positron emission tomography (PET) data by using scans of bone 
and soft tissue equivalent phantoms and scans of humans. This method of 
attenuation correction is intended for use in a single scanner that combines 
volume-imaging (3D) PET with x-ray computed tomography (CT) for the purpose of 
providing accurately registered anatomical localization of structures seen in 
the PET image. The goal of this work is to determine if we can perform 
attenuation correction of the PET emission data using accurately aligned CT 
attenuation information. We discuss possible methods of calculating the PET 
attenuation map at 511 keV based on CT transmission information acquired from 40 
keV through 140 keV. Data were acquired on separate CT and PET scanners and were 
aligned using standard image registration procedures. Results are presented on 
three of the attenuation calculation methods: segmentation, scaling, and our 
proposed hybrid segmentation/scaling method. The results are compared with those 
using the standard 3D PET attenuation correction method as a gold standard. We 
demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed hybrid method for converting the CT 
attenuation map from an effective CT photon energy of 70 keV to the PET photon 
energy of 511 keV. We conclude that using CT information is a feasible way to 
obtain attenuation correction factors for 3D PET.

DOI: 10.1118/1.598392
PMID: 9800714 [Indexed for MEDLINE]


2. Semin Nucl Med. 2003 Jul;33(3):166-79. doi: 10.1053/snuc.2003.127307.

X-ray-based attenuation correction for positron emission tomography/computed 
tomography scanners.

Kinahan PE(1), Hasegawa BH, Beyer T.

Author information:
(1)University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA.

A synergy of positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) 
scanners is the use of the CT data for x-ray-based attenuation correction of the 
PET emission data. Current methods of measuring transmission use positron 
sources, gamma-ray sources, or x-ray sources. Each of the types of transmission 
scans involves different trade-offs of noise versus bias, with positron 
transmission scans having the highest noise but lowest bias, whereas x-ray scans 
have negligible noise but the potential for increased quantitative errors. The 
use of x-ray-based attenuation correction, however, has other advantages, 
including a lack of bias introduced from post-injection transmission scanning, 
which is an important practical consideration for clinical scanners, as well as 
reduced scan times. The sensitivity of x-ray-based attenuation correction to 
artifacts and quantitative errors depends on the method of translating the CT 
image from the effective x-ray energy of approximately 70 keV to attenuation 
coefficients at the PET energy of 511 keV. These translation methods are usually 
based on segmentation and/or scaling techniques. Errors in the PET emission 
image arise from positional mismatches caused by patient motion or respiration 
differences between the PET and CT scans; incorrect calculation of attenuation 
coefficients for CT contrast agents or metallic implants; or keeping the 
patient's arms in the field of view, which leads to truncation and/or 
beam-hardening (or x-ray scatter) artifacts. Proper interpretation of PET 
emission images corrected for attenuation by using the CT image relies on an 
understanding of the potential artifacts. In cases where an artifact or bias is 
suspected, careful inspection of all three available images (CT and PET emission 
with and without attenuation correction) is recommended.

Copyright 2003 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

DOI: 10.1053/snuc.2003.127307
PMID: 12931319 [Indexed for MEDLINE]


3. Med Phys. 2006 Apr;33(4):976-83. doi: 10.1118/1.2174132.

Method for transforming CT images for attenuation correction in PET/CT imaging.

Carney JP(1), Townsend DW, Rappoport V, Bendriem B.

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicine, University of Tennessee Medical Center, Knoxville, TN 
37920, USA. carneyjp@upmc.edu

A tube-voltage-dependent scheme is presented for transforming Hounsfield units 
(HU) measured by different computed tomography (CT) scanners at different x-ray 
tube voltages (kVp) to 511 keV linear attenuation values for attenuation 
correction in positron emission tomography (PET) data reconstruction. A Gammex 
467 electron density CT phantom was imaged using a Siemens Sensation 16-slice 
CT, a Siemens Emotion 6-slice CT, a GE Lightspeed 16-slice CT, a Hitachi CXR 
4-slice CT, and a Toshiba Aquilion 16-slice CT at kVp ranging from 80 to 140 
kVp. All of these CT scanners are also available in combination with a PET 
scanner as a PET/CT tomograph. HU obtained for various reference tissue 
substitutes in the phantom were compared with the known linear attenuation 
values at 511 keV. The transformation, appropriate for lung, soft tissue, and 
bone, yields the function 9.6 x 10(-5). (HU+ 1000) below a threshold of 
approximately 50 HU and a (HU+ 1000)+b above the threshold, where a and b are 
fixed parameters that depend on the kVp setting. The use of the kVp-dependent 
scaling procedure leads to a significant improvement in reconstructed PET 
activity levels in phantom measurements, resolving errors of almost 40% 
otherwise seen for the case of dense bone phantoms at 80 kVp. Results are also 
presented for patient studies involving multiple CT scans at different kVp 
settings, which should all lead to the same 511 keV linear attenuation values. A 
linear fit to values obtained from 140 kVp CT images using the kVp-dependent 
scaling plotted as a function of the corresponding values obtained from 80 kVp 
CT images yielded y = 1.003 x -0.001 with an R2 value of 0.999, indicating that 
the same values are obtained to a high degree of accuracy.

DOI: 10.1118/1.2174132
PMID: 16696474 [Indexed for MEDLINE]


4. Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging. 2002 Jul;29(7):922-7. doi: 
10.1007/s00259-002-0796-3. Epub 2002 Apr 19.

PET attenuation coefficients from CT images: experimental evaluation of the 
transformation of CT into PET 511-keV attenuation coefficients.

Burger C(1), Goerres G, Schoenes S, Buck A, Lonn AH, Von Schulthess GK.

Author information:
(1)Nuclear Medicine, University Hospital, Rämistrasse 100, 8091 Zurich, 
Switzerland. burger@dmr.usz.ch

The CT data acquired in combined PET/CT studies provide a fast and essentially 
noiseless source for the correction of photon attenuation in PET emission data. 
To this end, the CT values relating to attenuation of photons in the range of 
40-140 keV must be transformed into linear attenuation coefficients at the PET 
energy of 511 keV. As attenuation depends on photon energy and the absorbing 
material, an accurate theoretical relation cannot be devised. The transformation 
implemented in the Discovery LS PET/CT scanner (GE Medical Systems, Milwaukee, 
Wis.) uses a bilinear function based on the attenuation of water and cortical 
bone at the CT and PET energies. The purpose of this study was to compare this 
transformation with experimental CT values and corresponding PET attenuation 
coefficients. In 14 patients, quantitative PET attenuation maps were calculated 
from germanium-68 transmission scans, and resolution-matched CT images were 
generated. A total of 114 volumes of interest were defined and the average PET 
attenuation coefficients and CT values measured. From the CT values the 
predicted PET attenuation coefficients were calculated using the bilinear 
transformation. When the transformation was based on the narrow-beam attenuation 
coefficient of water at 511 keV (0.096 cm(-1)), the predicted attenuation 
coefficients were higher in soft tissue than the measured values. This bias was 
reduced by replacing 0.096 cm(-1) in the transformation by the linear 
attenuation coefficient of 0.093 cm(-1) obtained from germanium-68 transmission 
scans. An analysis of the corrected emission activities shows that the resulting 
transformation is essentially equivalent to the transmission-based attenuation 
correction for human tissue. For non-human material, however, it may assign 
inaccurate attenuation coefficients which will also affect the correction in 
neighbouring tissue.

DOI: 10.1007/s00259-002-0796-3
PMID: 12111133 [Indexed for MEDLINE]----

      the values that are assigned to the pixels in a ct image are associated
with the attenuation of the corresponding tissue, or, more specifically, to their
linear attenuation coefficient  (m�1) (see section 2.3.1). the linear attenuation
coefficient depends on the composition of the material, the density of the material
and the photon energy, as seen in beer's law:

I(x) = I 0e-�x              (11.1)

where I(x) is the intensity of the attenuated X ray beam, I0 the unattenuated X ray
beam and x the thickness of the material. note that beer's law only describes
the attenuation of the primary beam and does not take into account the intensity
of scattered radiation that is generated. for use in polyenergetic X ray beams,
beer's law should strictly be integrated over all photon energies in the X ray
spectrum. however, in the back projection methodologies (see below) developed
for ct reconstruction algorithms, this is generally not implemented; instead,
typically, a pragmatic solution is to assume where beer's law can be applied
using one value representing the average photon energy of the X ray spectrum.
this assumption causes inaccuracies in the reconstruction and leads to the beam
hardening artefact.

intensities of the attenuated and unattenuated X ray beams, respectively I(d) and
I0, and that these can be measured. image reconstruction techniques can then be
applied to derive the matrix of linear attenuation coefficients, which is the basis
of the ct image.

11.2.2. Hounsfield units

      in the ct image, the matrix of reconstructed linear attenuation coefficients
(material) is transformed into a corresponding matrix of hounsfield units
(humaterial), where the hu scale is expressed relative to the linear attenuation
coefficient of water at room temperature (water):

      It can be seen that HUwater = 0 (material = water), HUair = �1000 (material = 0)
and HU = 1 is associated with 0.1% of the linear attenuation coefficient of water.
Table 11.1 shows typical values for body tissues. From the definition of the HU,
it follows that for all substances except water and air, variations of the HU values
occur when they are determined at different tube voltages. The reason is that, as
a function of photon energy, different substances exhibit a non-linear relationship
of their linear attenuation coefficient relative to that of water. This effect is most
notable for substances that have a relatively high effective atomic number, such
as contrast enhanced blood and bone.

      The minimum bit depth that should be assigned to a pixel is 12, enabling
the creation of a Hounsfield scale that ranges from �1024 HU to +3071 HU, thus
covering most clinically relevant tissues. A wider Hounsfield scale with a bit
depth of 14 is useful for extending the HU scale upwards to +15 359 HU, thus

making it compatible with materials that have a high density and a high linear
attenuation coefficient.

      CT images are usually visualized on a monitor using an eight bit greyscale
offering only 256 grey values. Each pixel HU value then has to undergo a linear
mapping to a `window' 8 bit value. The window width defines the range of HUs
that is represented by the mapped values (ranging from white to black) and the
window level defines the central HU value within the selected window width.
Optimal visualization of the tissues of interest in the image can only be achieved
by selecting the most appropriate window width and window level. Consequently,
different settings of the window width and window level are used to visualize
soft tissue, lung tissue or bone. The greyscale, as defined by window level and
window width, is adapted to the diagnostic task and is thus dependent on the
clinical question.

      In clinical practice, considerable deviations between the expected and the
observed HU values may occur. Causes for such inaccuracies may, for example, be
the dependence of the HU value on the reconstruction filter, the size of the scanned
field of view (FOV), and the position within the scanned FOV. In addition, image
artefacts may have an effect on the accuracy of the HU values. When performing
longitudinal clinical studies, one should take into account that, even for the same
scanner, the HU values for a given tissue type may vary with time. In multicentre
studies that involve different CT scanners, there may also be significant variations
in the observed HU values. Therefore, quantitative imaging in CT requires special
attention and often additional calibrations of the CT scanner.

11.3. The CT Imaging System

11.3.1. Historical and current acquisition configurations

      After preclinical research and development during the early 1970s, CT
developed rapidly as an indispensable imaging modality in diagnostic radiology
(Table 11.2). It is impressive to realize that most of the modern CT technology
that is being used in clinical practice nowadays had already been described by
the end of 1983 (Fig. 11.3). The development of multidetector row CT (MDCT)
and multisource CT had already been described in a US patent from 1980 [11.1].
The patent describes what the authors call "a multiple purpose high speed
tomographic X ray scanner". In the acquisition technique of helical CT (described
in Ref. [11.2]), the patent states that "the apparatus enables helical scanning to be
effected by the continuous transportation of the table couch". The helix is the
pathway of the continuously rotating X ray source seen from the perspective of
the patient.

                                                                                                  261
                                                        CHAPTER 11

   FIG.11.3. Concepts of multisource and MDCT scanning (left) and of helical CT (right).

      Volumetric CT with a scanner that was capable of imaging an entire volume
within a fraction of a second was achieved with the installation of the Dynamic
Spatial Reconstructor in 1980 at the Mayo Clinic in the USA. This scanner
used 14 X ray tubes and 14 image intensifiers and was capable of impressive
performance with regard to coverage and temporal resolution, even measured
against current standards.

      Currently, most scanners are helical MDCT scanners, but the technologies
of dual source and volumetric CT scanning have been implemented on a wide
scale.
11.3.2. Gantry and table

      The gantry contains all the system components that are required to record
transmission profiles of the patient. Since transmission profiles have to be
recorded at different angles, these components are mounted on a support within
the gantry that can be rotated. The X ray tube with high voltage generator and
tube cooling system, the collimator, the beam shaping filters, the detector arc and
the data acquisition system are all mounted on this support. The engineering of
these components is complex, since they need to be able to withstand the strong
centrifugal force that occurs during the fast rotation of the gantry. Forces of
several tens of g arise for rotation times of the order of 0.25 s.

      Electrical power is generally supplied to the rotating gantry by means of
slip ring contacts. Recorded projection profiles are generally transmitted from the
gantry to a computer by means of wireless communication technologies.

      The design and engineering of the table, as with the gantry, are critical to
allowing accurate acquisition of data at high rotational speeds. The table must

262
                                COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY

also be able to withstand heavy weights without bending. The position of the
patient on the table can be head first or feet first, and supine or prone; this position
is usually recorded with the scan data.

11.3.3. The X ray tube and generator
      Owing to the high X ray flux required for CT, the X ray tube uses a tungsten
anode designed to withstand and dissipate high heat loads. With long continuous
acquisition cycles, a forced cooling system using oil or water circulated through a
heat exchanger is often used.
11.3.4. Collimation and filtration
      The X ray beam should be collimated to the desired dimensions. The beam
width in the longitudinal axis is generally small; therefore, the collimated X ray
beam is often referred to as a fan beam. In the plane perpendicular to the table
motion, also known as the x�y or axial plane, the beam is shaped to reduce the
dynamic range of the signal that is recorded by the detectors. Beam shaping
(bowtie) filters are used to achieve the desired gradient, with one of a number of
mounted bowtie filters moved into the X ray beam during acquisition.
11.3.5. Detectors
      The essential physical characteristics of CT detectors are a good detection
efficiency and a fast response with little afterglow. Currently, solid state
detectors1 are used, as they have a detection efficiency close to 100% compared
with high pressure, xenon filled ionization chambers that were used previously
and that had a detection efficiency of about 70%. Solid state detectors are
generally scintilators, meaning that the X rays interacting with the detector
generate light. This light is converted to an electrical signal, by photodiodes that
are attached to the back of the scintillator, which should have good transparency
to ensure optimal detection. Typically, an antiscatter grid is mounted at the front
of the detector, which consists of small strips of highly attenuating material
(e.g. tungsten) aligned along the longitudinal (z) axis of the CT scanner, forming
a 1-D antiscatter grid.
      A detector row consists of thousands of dels that are separated by
septa designed to prevent light generated in one del from being detected by
neighbouring dels. These septa and the strips of the antiscatter grid should be
as small as possible since they reduce the effective area of the detector and thus
reduce the detection of X rays. Figure 11.4 shows detector modules for a 4, 16,
        1 This is a common term used for imaging detection to cover the use of scintillators and
photodiodes and should not be confused with thermoluminescent dosimeters (see Chapter 21
for further discussion).
264
                                            COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY
FIG.11.4. Detector modules for a 4, 16, 64 and 320 slice CT scanner (left). The complete CT
detector is composed of many detector modules (right) (courtesy Toshiba Medical Systems).
64 and 320 slice CT scanner. The complete CT detector is composed of many
detector modules that are mounted next to each other along an arc.
      CT detectors are curved in the axial (x�y) plane and rectangular along the
longitudinal (z) axis. While most dels are used to measure transmission profile
data (the attenuated intensity I(d)), the dels outside the FOV are used to measure
the unattenuated intensity of the X ray beam (I(0)). Thus, the coefficient I(d)/I(0)
from Eq. (11.2) can be easily recorded.
      The smallest size of an object (d) within the patient that can be resolved
in the reconstructed image depends on the number and size of dels along the
detector arc, the size of the dels along the z axis, the number of angles for which
projections are recorded during the acquisition, and the focal spot size of the X ray
tube. The minimum number of dels in a detector arc covering a specific FOV
should be approximately 2FOV/d, to resolve the object, d, in the reconstructed
image. About 800 dels are required to achieve a spatial resolution of 1 mm within
a reconstructed image for a FOV of 400 mm. Spatial resolution can be improved
for an acquisition with a full 360� rotation by a slight geometrical modification of
the arrangement of the dels. By shifting the dels by a distance equal to a quarter
of their size, the theoretically achievable spatial resolution becomes twice as
good. Thus, a quarter detector shift is generally implemented in CT scanners. As
a rule of thumb, the number of required projection angles can be approximated
by the number of required dels. With the current detector rows of 800�1000 dels,
covering an FOV of 400 mm, a spatial resolution of better than one millimetre
can be achieved.
      Figure 11.5 shows how coverage of MDCT scanners increased when
more active detector rows became available. A typical acquisition with a single
detector row scanner covered 5 mm. CT scanners with four active detector rows
achieved a substantial improvement of the longitudinal resolution. For example,
by using four active detector rows in a 4 � 1 mm acquisition configuration, the
longitudinal spatial resolution improved from 5 mm to 1.25 mm.
                                                                                                  265
                                                        CHAPTER 11
FIG.11.5. Coverage of the MDCT scanners increased when more active detector rows became
available.
      In clinical practice, CT scanners with four active detector rows were
primarily used to enhance longitudinal resolution, which allowed 3-D
visualization of the scanned volume. The CT scanners with four active detector
rows could also be used for enhanced longitudinal coverage, for example, by
selecting a 4 � 2 = 8 mm, or even a 4 � 4 = 16 mm coverage. Enhanced longitudinal
coverage would allow for shorter scan times but without the benefit of improved
longitudinal resolution. The CT scanners with 16 or 64 active detector rows
allowed for acquisitions in, for example, 16 � 0.5 = 8 mm and 64 � 0.5 = 32 mm
configurations. These scanners provided excellent longitudinal spatial resolution,
high quality 3-D reconstructions and, at the same time, reduced scan times. The
MDCT scanners with up to 64 active detector rows do not provide coverage of
entire organs, and to cover the prescribed range, the scan is generally a helical
acquisition with multiple rotations. With the 320 detector row CT scanner, one
single rotation allows for coverage of 160 mm, enough for covering organs such
as the brain or the heart within one single rotation.

The scale shown (Fig. 11) demonstrates the accuracy to which the absorp-
tion values can be ascertained on the picture. It shows the whole range of
the machine, from air (-1000) at the bottom of the scale, to bone at the top
of the scale, covering some 1 000 levels of absorption either side of water,
which has been chosen to be zero at the centre. (This is done for conve-
nience, as the absorption of water is close to that of tissue). To obtain
readings which relate to true absorption, 1000 must be added to these
readings, making air zero, and water would then be + 1000.

   The range of tones between black and white seen on the picture can be
restricted to a very small part of the scale. This "window" can be raised or
lowered according to the absorption value of the material we wish to
compare: for example, it must be raised to see the tissue of the heart or
lowered to see detail within the air of the lung. The sensitivity can be
able to reconstruct a picture from sets of very accurate X-ray measure-
ments taken through the body at a multitude of different angles. Many
hundreds of thousands of measurements would have to be taken, and
reconstructing a picture from them seemed to be a mammoth task as it
appeared at the time that it would require an equal number of many
hundreds of thousands of simultaneous equations to be solved.

    When I investigated the advantages over conventional X-ray techniques
however, it became apparent that the conventional methods were not
making full use of all the information the X-rays could give.

    On the other hand, calculations showed that the new system used the
data very efficiently and would be two orders of magnitude more sensitive
than conventional X-rays. For this reason I hoped that it would be possible
to distinguish between the various tissues of the body, although I could not
find any literature which suggested that such X-ray absorption differences
existed.

The Radiology 2023 review by Koetzier and colleagues is well covered in the results. The search did not return anything on the FDA clearance dates or on TrueFidelity or AiCE, so those parts of your query are unverified.

**The review:** Published in Radiology in March 2023 (vol. 306, no. 3, e221257), with Koetzier as first author and Willemink as corresponding author. The clinical introduction of deep learning reconstruction (DLR) algorithms over the past 5 years has demonstrated the potential of DLR to rapidly reconstruct images with low noise, desired noise texture, and preserved spatial resolution, and the authors report dose reductions of up to 71%.

**Technical principles:**
- Filtered back projection has been the standard for decades, but it struggles with noise and artifacts at lower doses (FBP has become increasingly obsolete as CT scanners grow faster and more advanced, and higher image noise is especially noticeable in lower-dose imaging).
- Model-based iterative reconstruction narrowed that gap, but its slow reconstruction and "plastic" image appearance limited adoption.
- Hybrid iterative reconstruction is described as the current state-of-the-art technique before DLR.
- DLR can be applied in the raw data domain, image domain, or both.

**Clinical prospects:**
- Compared with FBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, the review says DLR provides improved image quality.
- Deep learning–based metal artifact reduction has the potential to remove metal artifacts more accurately than current state-of-the-art MAR methods.
- The authors note that the performance of DLR algorithms relies on the quality of data used for model training, and that photon-counting CT may supply better training data and benefit spectral imaging.

**Not verified:** The search returned no information on the 2019 FDA clearance or on the TrueFidelity (GE) and AiCE (Canon) products. A follow-up search on those specific terms would be needed to confirm them.

The search turned up a few useful points, though no single source gives a complete 70–150 kV effective-energy table.

- **Mean energy rule of thumb:** One review states that the mean energy of the X-ray beam, in the unit of keV, is approximately between 1/3 and 1/2 of the kVp value. At 120 kVp, that implies roughly 40–60 keV.
- **Measured effective energy at 120 kVp:** A Heliyon study tabulates X-ray effective energy during CT scan at a tube voltage of 120 kVp, with one scanner listed at 55.74 keV. The snippet shows only that row, so I couldn't confirm the other scanners in that table.
- **Scanner differences:** One study notes that different clinical CT scanners have different X-ray spectra and photon energies, even at the same peak tube voltage (kVp) settings.
- **Available kV range:** On clinical scanners, 80 to 140 kVps in the increment of 20 kVp are typical offerings, but 70 and 150 kVp have become available on some newer models for advanced needs. A GE product comparison also lists several models with 70–150 kV ranges, though that table is hard to parse.
- **Low-kV contrast effect:** Iodine attenuation rises as kV falls, because the photon energy in the X-ray beam gets closer to the iodine k-edge (33 keV). A Siemens whitepaper compares iodine enhancement across 70–150 kV and notes that tube potentials between 70 and 100 kVp have been shown as most effective for contrast dose reduction.

The results don't include a direct 70–150 kV keV table, so for precise mean or effective energies at each kVp, you'd need the scanner's spectrum data or a dedicated spectral model such as TASMIP or SpekCalc.

Links: [{"title":"PET/CT Attenuation and its Artifact","url":"https://people.vcu.edu/~mhcrosthwait/PETW/PETCTattenuationcorrectionandartifacts.html"},{"title":"snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/37/3/441.full.pdf"},{"title":"jnm.snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/40/12/2025.full.pdf"},{"title":"snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/43/8/1054.full.pdf"},{"title":"snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals."},{"title":"jnm.snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/node/14771"},{"title":"jnm.snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/44/11/1855.full.pdf"},{"title":"jnm.snmjournals.org","url":"https://jnm.snmjournals.org/node/128349"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4277262"},{"title":"# **9 Artifacts in FDG PET and PET/CT**","url":"https://springerlink.bibliotecabuap.elogim.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-1-4419-0802-5_9"}]

The search returned several sources that describe this pattern. The short version: without attenuation correction, superficial and low-density tissue looks relatively hot, and deep structures look relatively cold.

- **Skin and lungs look hot:** One study reports apparent tracer activity at the skin surface because superficial photons are less attenuated (increased apparent tracer activity at the skin surface caused by limited superficial photon attenuation). In a non-attenuation-corrected whole-body FDG study, distinct activity is noted in the skin, lungs, liver and the renal region.
- **Deep structures look relatively cold:** A teaching resource notes that the lungs show increased activity, and that the inner parts of the body look "colder" relative to areas of lower density (Lungs show increased activity; inner portions of the body is "colder" in relationship to an increase in density). The same resource lists the lung/liver interface, skin surface, leg muscle, and central liver as areas to check on uncorrected images.
- **Strong activity in some organs is an artifact:** One study describes strong activity in the brain, renal pelvis, and bladder as a reconstruction artifact.
- **Mechanism:** Without correction, the reconstruction has to explain measured counts by assigning fewer counts to central projections, since central projections of the same activity produce fewer counts.
- **Thorax is a problem:** In non-uniform attenuation regions such as the thorax, foci of increased tracer uptake to "disappear" on non-corrected images. This means non-corrected images can miss real uptake, which is why some authors recommend reconstructing all studies with correction (all studies should at least be reconstructed with attenuation correction to avoid missing regions of elevated tracer uptake).
- **Practical use:** Non-AC images are commonly used to check for CT-based correction artifacts. One review notes that a relatively simple solution to diagnostic uncertainty regarding the presence of a CT-based AC artifact is to inspect the non-AC PET images.

Sources: the teaching page at people.vcu.edu, the JNM articles at jnm.snmjournals.org (content/37/3/441, content/jnumed/40/12/2025, content/43/8/1054, content/jnumed/44/11/1855, and the lookup link for the Bai/Hoffman work), and the PMC article PMC4277262. The one search returned these, so I did not verify the full texts. The VCU page is a teaching handout rather than a peer-reviewed source.

Different clinical CT scanners have different X-ray spectra and photon energies, even at the same peak tube voltage (kVp) settings. The search turned up consistent detector and coverage specs for the Aquilion ONE / INSIGHT Edition, but the rotation time varies by source.

- **Detector and coverage:** Canon's US product page lists a PUREINSIGHT detector with 320 rows at 0.5 mm and an 80 cm gantry bore. 16 cm z-axis coverage is confirmed by a MedicalExpo listing, which gives 16 cm z-axis coverage (wide‑area acquisition).
- **Rotation time:** Canon's current INSIGHT page lists 0.241 sec rotation speed. Another Canon page gives 0.24 sec with a footnote that the figure is an option. The 0.275 s figure you asked about appears on older material: a 2013 cardiology article describes the Aquilion One Vision Edition with a 0.275-second rotation. Canon's Aquilion Precision page also cites 0.275 sec rotation, but that is a different model.
- **Other sources:** A dealer listing for the Genesis Edition says its 16 cm wide-area coverage and 0.5 mm resolution allow you to scan large volumes in a single, fast rotation, without giving a rotation time. One third-party wiki page makes detailed claims about the detector with no clear sourcing, so I would not rely on it.

Bottom line: 320 rows × 0.5 mm, 16 cm coverage, and an 80 cm bore are well supported. The current rotation time is about 0.24 s, and 0.275 s reflects earlier Aquilion ONE generations. Canon's specs also note that design and specifications [are] subject to change without notice.

The search confirms the core specs, with one caveat: the 0.23 s rotation depends on the model tier.

- **Rotation speed:** The FDA 510(k) listing (K213715) describes the 0.23 s/rotation speed as a high-speed feature for cardiac imaging. Benefits: High-speed 0.23 s/rotation enables improved temporal resolution for cardiac imaging; spectral imaging aids in stone characterization. GE's own materials say the Revolution Apex Elite reaches 0.23 s, and that the Revolution Apex platform's Gemstone Clarity Detector allows upgrades from a 40 mm detector and 0.28-second rotation to 160 mm and 0.23 seconds. Another GE source says the system also offers 0.28 second rotation speed with the ability to increase to an 0.23 second rotation speed via an upgrade to Revolution Apex Elite.

- **Coverage and rows:** The FDA listing gives 160 mm detector coverage; 256 rows; 0.625 mm pixel pitch. A separate summary of the same family says configurations of 256 × 0.625mm rows, yielding up to 160mm coverage in the Z axis within a 320mm scan field of view.

- **Other specs:** GE lists 1300 mA of flux output in a 108 kW package and up to 437.5 mm/s volumetric scanning reconstructed to a maximum 50 cm field-of-view (FOV). Its one-beat cardiac claim is marketing: the Revolution Apex Elite is able to achieve unlimited 1-beat cardiac with 0.23s rotation speeds at a 19.5 ms temporal resolution.

- **Tier caveat:** A GE GoldSeal configuration sheet lists a standard Apex with 0.28 second Rotation, 1,200 mA output and 160 mm z-coverage. So a 160 mm, 256-row system is not automatically 0.23 s; check the specific model.

Mean Hounsfield unit measurements obtained on the Definition AS Plus scanner were lower than those obtained on the Volume CT scanner, with the intriguing exception of the anterior midline subcutaneous fat Hounsfield unit measurements, which were higher on the Definition AS Plus scanner. Links: [{"title":"Enhancement of Anemia Detection by Correlating Computed Tomography Findings of Abdominal Aorta and Inferior Vena Cava With Laboratory Investigations","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9816921/"},{"title":"Diagnostic Utility of Non-contrast Thoracic Computed Tomography in the Detection of Anemia and Its Severity: A Cross-Sectional Analytical Study","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12426566/"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9741598"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9816921"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/201167653.pdf"},{"title":"katalog.lib.cas.cz","url":"https://katalog.lib.cas.cz/KNAV/EdsRecord/cmedm,36627998"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8359593"},{"title":"nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8128794"},{"title":"s00330 020 07497 y","url":"https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00330-020-07497-y"},{"title":"Back to Search","url":"https://searchworks.jioinstitute.edu.in/articles/asx__9160526"}]

The search turned up useful background, but no study that sets a 35 HU threshold specifically for the aorta.

- **Mean aortic value:** In a retrospective study of 423 patients with abdominal unenhanced CT, the mean attenuation was 37.7 HU in the aorta and 36.1 HU in the IVC, and the authors tested how these values correlate with hemoglobin (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9816921/).
- **Thoracic study:** A cross-sectional study of unenhanced thoracic CT reported lower blood attenuation in anemic patients across several vessels, including the aortic arch (about +33.4 vs. +45.2 HU in non-anemic patients) and the ascending aorta (about +35.2 vs. +45.1 HU) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12426566/).
- **Where the 35 HU figure appears:** A 2019 Belgian radiology image article attributes the <35 HU cutoff to the superior sagittal sinus or left ventricle, not the aorta, and says that an aortic value above 50 HU in males and 45 HU in females suggests no anemia (https://core.ac.uk/download/201167653.pdf).
- **Caveat on cutoffs:** Another thoracic CT study states that there is no reliable cut-off for blood attenuation to suggest anemia on the non-contrast chest CT. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9741598)

Bottom line: the aortic mean values in the literature cluster around 35–45 HU, and the 35 HU threshold is documented for other chambers or sinuses rather than the aorta. Studies also disagree on whether a fixed cutoff is reliable.

Web search results for query: "normal lung attenuation Hounsfield units inspiration mean lung density -850 HU healthy adults CT expiration"

Links: [{"title":"www.pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://www.pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22836310/"},{"title":"www.sinapse.ac.uk","url":"https://www.sinapse.ac.uk/?p=3319"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3703944"},{"title":"quantitative computed tomography lungs and airways healthy nonsmoking adults","url":"https://lmi.bwh.harvard.edu/lmi/publications/quantitative-computed-tomography-lungs-and-airways-healthy-nonsmoking-adults"},{"title":"synapse.koreamed.org","url":"https://synapse.koreamed.org/articles/1027373"},{"title":"Back to Search","url":"https://searchworks.jioinstitute.edu.in/articles/edsair__edsair.doi...........39914a7a16057602dc69db26d67cde63"},{"title":"publications.ersnet.org","url":"https://publications.ersnet.org/content/erj/49/1/1600345"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5736979/figure/fig1"},{"title":"Journal List > J Korean Soc Radiol > v.67(5) > 1087183","url":"https://synapse.koreamed.org/articles/1087183"},{"title":"koreamed.org","url":"https://synapse.koreamed.org/articles/1067871"}]

The search didn't turn up a single "normal" mean lung density of -850 HU for healthy adults. The closest figures come from a few studies, and they vary with the breathing phase and the study population.

- **Inspiration:** A Korean study of 36 healthy nonsmokers with normal lung function reported an upper normal limit for mean lung density of -837.58 HU on inspiration CT. The same abstract's expiratory value reads "686.82 HU," which is almost certainly a typo, so I wouldn't rely on it.
- **Mean values by group:** An ERJ study of 45–65-year-old never-smokers, smokers, and COPD patients reported mean lung attenuation of −776±40 HU at expiration and −874±20 HU at inspiration for one group. The table layout suggests that column is the healthy never-smokers, but the header wasn't visible, so please check the original.
- **Study design:** The COPDGene analysis of 92 healthy non-Hispanic White nonsmokers scanned at full inspiration and at the end of a normal expiration. That study also found that mean (SD) %LAA(I-950) was 3.6% (3.2%) in men, compared with 1.3% (2.0%) in women, and that these attenuation differences by age and sex do not persist on multivariate analysis.
- **Sources of variation:** Depth of breathing and scanner type are potential sources of variation in measurement of attenuation-based quantitative CT parameters. Protocols also differ, so values from different scanners and kernels aren't directly interchangeable.

For a -850 HU reference, the best option is to pull the mean and SD from a healthy-nonsmoker cohort scanned on a comparable protocol, such as the COPDGene paper (Zach et al., Invest Radiol 2012) or the Korean study, and check whether the value is for inspiration or expiration.

filters. CT scanners offer many reconstruction filters that are optimized for specific
clinical purposes. It is possible to reconstruct one single CT scan with different
reconstruction filters, in order to optimize the visualization of, for example, both
bone and soft tissue.
      Other reconstruction techniques such as algebraic or iterative reconstruction
can also be used in CT. An algebraic reconstruction may seem attractive; however,
algebraic reconstruction through equation solving is not feasible in clinical
practice, owing to the large (512 � 512) matrices that are used in medical imaging
and to inconsistencies in the equations from measurement errors and noise.
      Iterative (statistical) reconstructions are now commonly used in CT. The
iterative reconstruction is well known in medical imaging, since it is routinely
used in nuclear medicine. Iterative techniques provide potential benefits in CT,
including the removal of streak artefacts (particularly when fewer projection
angles are used), and better performance in low dose CT acquisitions. However,
iteratively reconstructed images may be affected by artefacts that are not present
in filtered back projection images, such as aliasing patterns and overshoots in
the areas of sharp intensity transitions. Iterative reconstruction algorithms are
becoming popular in commercial CT scanners and can produce low noise images.

- **0.26 g/cm³ appears in a phantom context.** A CDC document on the Livermore Thoracic Phantom says its mock lungs had to have a density of 0.26 gm cmP3. It also ties that formulation to ICRU Report 44, noting that this formulation is identified as Griffith Lung in ICRU Report No. 44 (1989). This is a lung-substitute material spec, not a reference tissue density.
- **ICRU 44 lists lung as deflated.** A comparison table gives the ICRU 44 density for Lung (deflated) as 1.05 g/cm³, which is a different tissue-density convention from the inflated lung value you're asking about.
- **ICRP 89 lung values in phantom work differ.** A dosimetry paper lists lung density as 0.38 with a "calculated" comment, and another phantom paper assumed a homogeneous lung (soft tissue and air at 0.296 g cm�3).

The 0.26 figure seems to come from the Livermore phantom's lung-substitute specification, while the ICRU 44 table uses a deflated-lung density. To confirm whether ICRU 44 or ICRP 89 lists an inflated lung density of 0.26, check the original tables directly.

- ct-tube-voltage | A CT scanner runs its X-ray tube at a peak voltage between about 70 and 150 kilovolts, and 120 kilovolts is the usual setting for adult body scans.
- ct-beam-energy-spectrum | The beam is a mix of photon energies up to the tube voltage (up to 120 keV at 120 kV), and on average it behaves like a single-energy beam of roughly 55 to 70 keV.
- beer-lambert-law | The number of photons that get straight through a material falls off exponentially with thickness: I = I0 x exp(-mu x d), where I0 is the number going in, d is the thickness and mu is the linear attenuation coefficient of the material.
- water-attenuation-70-and-511-kev | One centimeter of water removes about 18 percent of 70 keV X-ray photons from the beam (mu about 0.19 per cm) but only about 9 percent of the 511 keV photons used in PET (mu about 0.096 per cm).
- attenuation-table-materials | At CT energies, one centimeter of dense bone removes about 39 percent of the X-ray photons from the beam, water or muscle about 18 percent, fat about 16 percent, air-filled lung about 5 percent, and air almost none.
- bone-vs-water-attenuation-ratio | Dense bone attenuates 70 keV X-rays about 2.6 times as strongly as water, but 511 keV PET photons only about 1.8 times as strongly.
- transmission-through-water-70-kev | Of 100 X-ray photons at 70 keV aimed into water, about 82 pass straight through 1 cm, 38 through 5 cm, 14 through 10 cm and only 2 through 20 cm.
- transmission-through-bone-and-lung-70-kev | About 61 percent of 70 keV photons pass straight through 1 cm of dense bone and about 8 percent through 5 cm, while about 61 percent pass through 10 cm of air-filled lung.
- hounsfield-unit-definition | CT images are stored in Hounsfield units, which compare each tissue with water: HU = 1000 x (mu - mu_water) / mu_water, so 1 HU is a 0.1 percent difference from water.
- hounsfield-air-and-water | On the Hounsfield scale water is 0 and air is -1000.
- hounsfield-lung | Air-filled lung measures about -950 to -600 HU, because it is mostly air.
- hounsfield-fat | Fat measures about -100 HU, slightly below water, typically between -130 and -70 HU.
- hounsfield-blood | Blood without contrast agent measures roughly +30 to +60 HU, a little above water.
- hounsfield-muscle | Muscle measures roughly +10 to +65 HU, most often about +40 to +50 HU.
- hounsfield-liver | A healthy liver measures about +45 to +70 HU without contrast agent, and fat in the liver lowers the number.
- hounsfield-spongy-bone | Spongy bone, such as the inside of a vertebra, varies widely with age and bone health, from under +100 HU to +300 HU or more.
- hounsfield-cortical-bone | Dense compact bone measures from several hundred HU to +2000 HU or more, typically around +1000 to +1500 HU.
- ct-gantry-rotation-time | Inside the ring, the X-ray tube and the detector opposite it spin around the patient about two to four times every second.
- ct-detector-rows | Instead of one row of detector elements, a modern CT scanner has many rows side by side, commonly 64 and up to 320, so each turn records a band of the body rather than a single thin slice.
- ct-slice-thickness | The thinnest slices on most current scanners are about 0.5 to 0.625 mm, and the newest photon-counting scanners reach 0.2 mm.
- ct-whole-body-scan-time | The CT part of a PET/CT exam, which usually covers the body from the head or neck to the thighs, takes well under a minute.
- why-bone-stops-more-x-rays | Bone stops more X-rays than soft tissue for two reasons: it is nearly twice as dense, and about a third of its weight is calcium and phosphorus, heavier atoms that absorb X-ray photons outright far more readily than the hydrogen, carbon and oxygen of soft tissue.
- soft-tissue-mostly-scatters | Soft tissues are mostly water, differ from water by only a few percent in how strongly they attenuate X-rays, and at CT energies about nine out of ten of their interactions with X-ray photons are Compton scattering.
- three-fates-of-an-x-ray-photon | Each X-ray photon entering the body does one of three things: it passes straight through and reaches the detector, it is absorbed by an atom and disappears (the photoelectric effect), or it bounces off an electron in a new direction (scattering).
- photons-do-not-slow-down | X-ray photons do not slow down in the body; they all travel at the speed of light, and tissue only reduces how many of them arrive, which is what attenuation means.
- radon-transform | The mathematics behind CT goes back to 1917, when the mathematician Johann Radon showed that a two-dimensional pattern can be recovered from the sums measured along all the straight lines crossing it; the set of those line sums is now called the Radon transform.
- filtered-back-projection | For about four decades the standard way to turn the measurements into a picture was filtered back-projection: each measured profile is sharpened with a "ramp" filter and then smeared back across the image along the direction it was measured from, and the smears from all angles add up to the cross-section.
- first-ct-used-iterative-reconstruction | The first CT scanners of the early 1970s built their images with a step-by-step (iterative) method, but the computers of the time were too slow for it and filtered back-projection soon replaced it.
- iterative-reconstruction-return | Since about 2009, faster computers have let scanner makers bring back iterative reconstruction, which repeatedly adjusts the image until it agrees with the measurements and gives cleaner pictures at lower radiation dose; it is now common.
- deep-learning-reconstruction | The newest method, deep-learning reconstruction, uses a neural network trained on pairs of lower-quality and higher-quality scans to produce low-noise images; the first such products for CT were cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2019.
- ct-based-attenuation-correction | In a PET/CT scanner the CT image does a second job: it is converted into a map of how strongly each part of the body attenuates 511 keV photons, and that map is used to correct the PET data for the photon pairs that were absorbed or scattered inside the patient.
- ct-to-511-kev-conversion | Because CT measures attenuation at about 70 keV and PET needs it at 511 keV, the scanner rescales every pixel, using one straight-line conversion for air, lung and soft tissue and a second, less steep line for bone.
- kinahan-1998-reference | A 1998 paper in the journal Medical Physics by Paul Kinahan, David Townsend, Thomas Beyer and Donald Sashin showed, using CT and PET scans of test objects and of people, that a CT image can be used to correct PET data for attenuation in a combined PET/CT scanner.
- pet-without-attenuation-correction | Without attenuation correction a PET image is misleading in a recognizable way: the skin and the lungs look too bright, and the deep center of the body looks too dim.
- photon-pair-loss-in-the-body | A PET event is counted only if both 511 keV photons escape the body, and along a line through 30 cm of tissue only about 1 pair in 18 does, so the correction is large.

input.summary: The draft has 35 claims (all status "unverified") plus attenuation, transmission, Hounsfield, interaction and photon-pair tables, with every derived number computed by scripts/build_draft.js in the same scratch folder; water at 511 keV is confirmed at 0.096 per cm from NIST and three PET papers. Main corrections: effective beam energy at 120 kV is roughly 55 to 70 keV, not 60 to 70; spongy bone is about +100 to +300 HU in vertebrae, and I found no primary source for the draft's +300 to +400; Kinahan 1998 proposed a hybrid segmentation/scaling method, while bilinear scaling comes from Burger 2002 and Carney 2006; the IAEA Hounsfield formula divides by mu_water alone; blood, muscle, fat and liver ranges were widened or shifted because the IAEA table and measured patient data disagree. Additions: the first CT scanners used iterative reconstruction before filtered back-projection, Rayleigh scatter is a minor third interaction, and Compton scatter is still the most common interaction in bone at 70 keV (62 percent, against 30 percent photoelectric). Still doubtful: the 0.26 g/cm3 inflated-lung density could not be traced to a primary source I could open; log-log interpolation at 70 keV runs 0.2 to 1.8 percent above NIST XCOM's direct values (both are in the table, and thick-bone transmission is sensitive to it); "first iterative product in 2009" may be contradicted by a 2008 GE product I did not verify; several plain-language ranges (spongy bone upper end, liver lower end, "commonly 64 rows") are my own summaries and are flagged in the notes.
